subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Bubble Tea: Taiwan's Sweet Invention
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bubble Tea: Taiwan's Sweet Invention usable.

hook.text: Bubble tea was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s when someone added tapioca pearls to iced milk tea—and created a global craze.

buildup.text: Two Taiwanese tea shops both claim the invention. Chun Shui Tang and Hanlin Tea Room have disputed credit for decades.

discovery.text: The chewy tapioca pearls (called 'boba') transformed tea from a simple drink into an interactive, textural experience.

twist.text: A Taiwanese court ruled in 2019 that bubble tea cannot be patented—it's too simple. No one owns the invention.

climax.text: Bubble tea is now a multi-billion dollar global industry. From Taipei to London, boba shops outnumber many traditional cafés.

punchline.text: Tapioca in tea—simple, addictive, unstoppable. A snack-drink conquered the world.

quiz.question: Where was bubble tea invented?
options: Taiwan in the 1980s when tapioca pearls were added to iced milk tea

details.summary: Bubble tea was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s when tea shops began adding chewy tapioca balls to iced tea drinks. Two shops, Chun Shui Tang and Hanlin Tea Room, both claim credit. The drink spread across Asia in the 1990s and has since become a global phenomenon.
details.whyItMatters: Bubble tea is the most successful tea innovation of the modern era, proving that tea culture can evolve and capture entirely new generations of drinkers.
takeaways: Bubble tea originated in Taiwan in the 1980s
Chewy tapioca pearls in iced tea defined the new category
It became a global phenomenon reaching every continent

faq.question: What are the tapioca pearls in bubble tea made from?
faq.answer: The pearls are made from tapioca starch derived from cassava root. They are formed into small balls, cooked until chewy, and often soaked in sugar syrup for sweetness. Their distinctive texture is what makes bubble tea unique.

faq.question: How did bubble tea spread from Taiwan to become a global phenomenon?
faq.answer: Taiwanese diaspora communities opened boba shops across Asia, then North America and Europe. Social media accelerated the trend in the 2010s, making the colorful, photogenic drinks viral hits among younger consumers worldwide.
